title: Regiment and Letter
premise: In 1847, apprentice clockmaker Coral Thornbury is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock and discovers hidden inside its case a bundle of letters from Aldous Vane, a cartographer now declared an enemy of the state, addressed to her late father — letters that prove a magistrate framed Vane for treason to seize his survey maps. Bound by a promise her father made in peacetime, Coral must smuggle the evidence past the census taker who serves the magistrate, while the clock's failing mechanism becomes both her cover and her countdown. She repairs the clock, delivers the truth to a sympathetic judge at the cost of her apprenticeship, and watches Vane exonerated though never restored — learning that justice kept outside the law leaves scars memory alone must carry.
about_author: L. M. Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing provincial court records before turning to fiction. They write quiet historical thrillers about ordinary tradespeople caught in machinery far larger than themselves.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. During the national census, the taker Mr. Quill asks not only household names but whether her father ever corresponded with 'persons of foreign commission.' Coral lies smoothly, but that night she finds the observatory summons bearing Quill's countersignature. The beat: unease disguised as routine, the sense that silence itself has become dangerous.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes Slow
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. In the observatory tower she diagnoses the master clock's fault and finds letters sewn into the weight chamber — her father's hand, and Vane's. Reading them, she learns of the framed treason and her father's promise to hold the proof safe. Beat: grief rekindled into resolve; the past stops being past.

chapters.title: What the Father Kept
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, interleaved with letter excerpts. She pieces together the story: Vane mapped the coast, Magistrate Halloway claimed the charts as his own discovery, and when Vane objected he was branded an enemy agent. Her father hid the originals in the clock. Beat: the terrible clarity of understanding why her father taught her which silences keep people safe.

chapters.title: The Census Taker's Rounds
chapters.summary: Quill's POV. We see him as more than a functionary: ambitious, indebted to Halloway, genuinely convinced he protects order. He notes Coral's tenancy irregularities and requests her workshop papers. Beat: cold dread from the antagonist's side; the net tightening through paperwork, not violence.

chapters.title: Apprentice's Hands
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She copies the key letters onto tissue paper, hiding fragments inside clock cases awaiting repair around the city — distributing risk the way her father distributed silences. Her master notices her distraction and warns her that clocks forgive nothing. Beat: resourcefulness shadowed by isolation; she can trust no one fully.

chapters.title: A Debt in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Vane's POV, from the coastal prison depot where enemy persons are held. He remembers the promise made over brandy years ago and writes one last petition, unaware it will be intercepted. Beat: dignity under erasure; a man becoming a name on a list, holding onto memory as his only property.

chapters.title: The Weight Chamber
chapters.summary: Quill's POV. Searching the observatory on Halloway's orders, he finds the clock empty of letters but notices fresh oil on the weight chamber — someone has been inside it recently. He begins mapping every clock Coral's workshop has serviced. Beat: the hunter's patience; Coral's cleverness has left a trail.

chapters.title: Running Down
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. One hidden copy is seized; a fellow apprentice is questioned and breaks. Cornered, Coral retrieves the original letters and races toward Judge Ellery, the one magistrate Halloway cannot intimidate — while Quill follows the trail of oiled movements through the city. Beat: full flight, the countdown literalized in striking clocks marking her progress.

chapters.title: The Hour Hand Falls
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating Coral and Quill POVs. At the observatory, Quill corners Coral among the gears; she triggers the master clock's escapement, jamming the mechanism so the tower bell strikes wrong across the city — drawing a crowd, witnesses, and Ellery himself, whom she'd secretly summoned. She surrenders the letters publicly. Beat: courage as timing; justice arriving through noise instead of silence.

chapters.title: What Memory Keeps
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, months later. Vane is exonerated but barred from his profession; Halloway resigns rather than face trial; Coral loses her indenture but gains her own small shop, where Vane brings her a broken watch to mend. The repaired master clock keeps perfect time above them. Beat: bittersweet resolution — the law was too slow, but memory, like a good movement, held.
